Seed germination in a perennial grass species depends on both soil temperature and soil moisture. To measure these effects, researchers placed 50 seeds in each of several dishes filled with sterilized soil. Soil moisture was set by adding water equal to a fixed percentage of the dry soil mass (for example, 20% moisture means 20 g of water per 100 g of dry soil) and was maintained daily by weighing each dish and replacing any water lost. Dishes were kept in dark incubators, each held at a single constant temperature, across a range of temperatures and soil-moisture levels. Three dishes were prepared for every combination of temperature and moisture.

A seed was counted as germinated once its root had emerged at least 2 mm from the seed coat. After 14 days, the number of germinated seeds in each dish was recorded, and the percent germination for each combination was calculated as the total number of germinated seeds divided by the total number of seeds, multiplied by 100. The results are shown in Table 1.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Percent germination after 14 days at each soil temperature (rows) and soil-moisture level (columns).

prompt: According to Table 1, at a soil temperature of 25 °C and a soil-moisture level of 20%, the percent germination was:
explanation: In the 25 °C row of Table 1, the value under 20% moisture is 92%. The values 73% and 84% are the 10% and 30% moisture results in the same row, and 78% is the 20% moisture result at 20 °C.

The solubility of a salt in water is the maximum mass of the salt that will dissolve in 100 g of water at a given temperature, producing a saturated solution. Chemists measured the solubility of three salts, Salt X, Salt Y, and Salt Z, at each of several temperatures.

For each measurement, 100 g of distilled water was placed in a flask held in a water bath at the chosen temperature. The salt was added in small portions with stirring until a small amount of undissolved solid remained at the bottom of the flask for 10 minutes. The solution was then quickly filtered at the same temperature to remove the undissolved solid, and the filtered solution was heated to evaporate the water. The mass of the dry salt left behind was recorded as the solubility at that temperature, in grams of salt per 100 g of water. Each measurement was repeated three times, and the averages are shown in Table 1.

explanation: In the 40 °C row of Table 1, the Salt Y column reads 63.8, so the solubility was "63.8 g per 100 g of water." The value 36.5 is Salt X at the same temperature; 31.5 and 110.2 are Salt Y at 20 °C and 60 °C.

Sound intensity is the power carried by a sound wave per unit area. Sound level, measured in decibels (dB), is a logarithmic scale of intensity: every decrease of 10 dB corresponds to a tenfold decrease in sound intensity, so a decrease of 20 dB corresponds to a decrease in intensity by a factor of 100.

Students investigated how well flat panels of different materials block sound. A speaker in one chamber produced a steady 1,000 Hz tone, and a sound-level meter was placed in a second chamber, 1.0 m from the speaker. The two chambers were separated by a rigid wall with a square opening into which a panel could be clamped. With the opening empty, the meter read 90 dB. The students then clamped panels of foam, pine wood, and steel, each made in more than one thickness, into the opening one at a time. For each panel, the sound reduction was calculated as 90 dB minus the sound level read by the meter with that panel in place. The speaker's volume setting, the tone frequency, and the meter's position were the same for every panel. The results are shown in Figure 1.

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Sound reduction, in dB, for each panel tested.

prompt: According to Figure 1, the sound reduction produced by the 4 cm pine panel was:
choices: 22 dB
24 dB
30 dB
34 dB
correct_answer: 30 dB
explanation: The bar labeled "Pine, 4 cm" in Figure 1 reaches "30 dB." The 24 dB bar is the 2 cm pine panel, 22 dB is the 4 cm foam panel, and 34 dB is the 2 cm steel panel.
subskill: read a value from a bar graph

Limnologists describe a stratified lake in three layers: the epilimnion, a warm upper layer of nearly uniform temperature; the thermocline, the depth range over which temperature changes most rapidly with depth; and the hypolimnion, a cold bottom layer of nearly uniform temperature.

To study a 20 m deep lake, researchers anchored a boat over the deepest point and lowered a temperature probe on a marked cable, recording the water temperature at regular depth intervals from the surface to the bottom. The same procedure was carried out at midday on one day in July and again on one day in October of the same year. Air temperature and wind speed were also recorded but are not shown. Figure 1 shows the water temperature, in °C, measured at each depth on the two dates.

Calcium carbonate (CaCO3) tablets react with hydrochloric acid (HCl) to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and dissolved calcium chloride. The rate of this reaction can be compared by measuring the time required for a tablet to dissolve completely. Students performed three experiments using tablets that each had a mass of 1.0 g. In every trial, the tablet was added to 100 mL of HCl in a beaker, the acid was stirred at 200 rpm, and the time from when the tablet entered the acid until no solid remained was recorded as the dissolution time.

Experiment 1
A whole tablet was dropped into 1.0 mol/L HCl that had been brought to 10 °C in a water bath. The procedure was repeated with fresh acid at 20 °C, 30 °C, and 40 °C. The results are shown in Table 1.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated at 20 °C only, except that the tablet was used in one of three forms: whole, broken into 4 roughly equal pieces, or crushed into a powder. The results are shown in Table 1.

Experiment 3
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated at 20 °C with whole tablets, except that the concentration of the HCl was 0.25 mol/L, 0.50 mol/L, 1.0 mol/L, or 2.0 mol/L. The results are shown in Table 1.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Dissolution time of a 1.0 g CaCO3 tablet in 100 mL of HCl stirred at 200 rpm.

prompt: Which of the following factors was varied in Experiment 2 but held constant in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 3?
choices: The temperature of the HCl solution
The form of the tablet
The concentration of the HCl solution
The stirring rate
correct_answer: The form of the tablet
explanation: Only Experiment 2 tested whole, 4-piece, and powdered tablets; Experiments 1 and 3 used whole tablets throughout. Temperature was varied in Experiment 1, HCl concentration in Experiment 3, and the stirring rate was 200 rpm in every trial.
subskill: identify the independent variable of an experiment

The infiltration rate of a soil is the rate at which water on the soil surface enters the soil. Students measured infiltration rates in a field that contained plots of three soil textures: sand, loam, and clay. In each trial, a metal ring 15 cm in diameter was pushed 5 cm into the soil, 500 mL of water was poured into the ring, and the time until no water remained on the surface was recorded. The infiltration rate, in millimeters per hour (mm/h), was calculated from the depth of water in the ring and the recorded time. Each trial was repeated 3 times at nearby locations within the same area, and the average is reported.

Experiment 1
No rain had fallen for 7 days before the trials, and none of the plots had been walked on or driven over during the previous month. One trial was performed on each of the sand, loam, and clay plots. The results are shown in Figure 1.

Experiment 2
On the same day as Experiment 1, three additional areas of the loam plot were selected. A lawn roller with a mass of 50 kg was pushed across one area 10 times and across another area 20 times; the third area received 0 passes. A trial was then performed on each area. The results are shown in Figure 1.

Experiment 3
On the same day, an additional area of the loam plot that had not been compacted was pre-wetted by pouring 2 L of water evenly over it. One hour later, a trial was performed on this area. The results are shown in Figure 1.

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Average infiltration rate for each trial. Experiment 1: Sand, Loam, Clay. Experiment 2: loam after 0, 10, and 20 roller passes (L-0, L-10, L-20). Experiment 3: pre-wetted loam (L-wet).

prompt: Based on the results of Experiment 1, the infiltration rate of the loam plot was approximately how many times the infiltration rate of the clay plot?
explanation: In Figure 1, the loam bar in Experiment 1 is about 75 mm/h and the clay bar about 25 mm/h, so loam infiltrated about "3" times as fast as clay.
subskill: compare bar heights as a ratio

Soil respiration is the release of carbon dioxide (CO₂) from soil, mostly by microorganisms that break down organic matter. Students investigated how temperature, moisture, and the supply of organic carbon affect the rate of soil respiration.

In each trial, a 200 g core of soil collected from a single meadow was placed in a sealed 1 L glass jar. After 24 hours, the CO₂ concentration in the air inside the jar was measured with an infrared gas analyzer and converted to a CO₂ flux, in milligrams of CO₂ per kilogram of soil per hour (mg/kg/h).

Study 1
Four cores were adjusted to a moisture content of 25% by mass and incubated at 5 °C, 15 °C, 25 °C, or 35 °C (Trials 1-4, Table 1).

Study 2
Five cores were incubated at 25 °C after being adjusted to a moisture content of 5%, 15%, 25%, 35%, or 45% by mass (Trials 5-9).

Study 3
Four cores were adjusted to 25% moisture and incubated at 25 °C. Before incubation, 1.0 g of glucose dissolved in 5 mL of water was mixed into two of the cores; 5 mL of water alone was mixed into the other two. One core from each pair was first autoclaved (heated under pressure to 121 °C for 30 min) and allowed to cool before anything was mixed in (Trials 10-13).

passage:
A space probe surveyed the narrow ring that circles a giant planet. The ring orbits 1.6 planetary radii from the planet's center, inside the distance at which tidal forces prevent loose material from gathering into a moon. Its particles are more than 90% water ice by mass, its total mass is about 10^16 kg, and two small moons orbit just inside and just outside its edges. Two scientists discuss how the ring formed.

Scientist 1

The ring is young, no more than 10 million years old. A small icy moon drifted inside the tidal limit and was torn apart; the two moons at the ring's edges are its largest surviving pieces, and they keep the ring narrow. Fresh debris is bright, nearly pure ice, and it darkens as meteoroid dust settles on it at a known rate. The probe measured the ring's reflectivity at 0.6, comparable to fresh frost, whereas the planet's oldest icy moons reflect less than 0.3. At the known dust rate, a surface that bright cannot have been exposed for more than a few tens of millions of years.

Scientist 2

The ring is primordial: material left over from the planet's formation 4.5 billion years ago that never gathered into a moon because it lies inside the tidal limit. The edge moons formed at the same time and have confined the ring ever since, so its narrowness says nothing about its age. Neither does its brightness. Ring particles collide constantly, and each collision chips off the darkened outer layer and exposes clean ice, so a continually resurfaced ring stays bright indefinitely. Dust that fell on the ring over billions of years should instead be mixed through the particles' interiors. The probe's spectrometer found about 2% silicate dust by mass distributed through the ring particles, several times more than a 10-million-year-old ring could have collected.
prompt: Scientist 1 and Scientist 2 would most likely agree with which of the following statements about the ring?
choices: It formed when an icy moon was torn apart inside the tidal limit.
The two small moons at its edges keep it from spreading.
Its brightness shows that its particles were exposed recently.
It contains more silicate dust than a young ring could have collected.
correct_answer: The two small moons at its edges keep it from spreading.
explanation: Scientist 1 says the edge moons "keep the ring narrow" and Scientist 2 says they "have confined the ring ever since." The shattered-moon origin and the reading of the brightness as youth belong to Scientist 1 alone; the dust argument belongs to Scientist 2 alone.
domain: Evaluation of Models, Inferences, and Experimental Results

passage_title: A Summer Fever in a Farming Valley
passage:
For six summers, residents of a farming valley have suffered an illness marked by fever, joint pain, and rash. Cases occur only from July through September; nearly all patients live within 2 km of the valley's river; a previously unknown virus can be isolated from patients' blood; and the same virus is present in the blood of the valley's cattle, which show no signs of disease. Three scientists propose how the virus reaches people.

Scientist 1

The virus is carried by biting midges that breed in flooded irrigation ditches along the river. Midges feed on cattle and on people at dusk, and the virus multiplies in a midge for several days. Cases should be fewest in years when the ditches are drained early, and people who spend evenings outdoors should be at greatest risk. Traps set within 500 m of the ditches collected 20 times as many midges as traps set 2 km away, and pooled midges from the ditch-side traps contained the virus.

Scientist 2

The virus is carried by ticks that feed on cattle. A tick picks up the virus from a cow and passes it to a person who handles cattle or walks through pasture. The late-summer timing of cases matches the activity peak of the tick's adult stage. Cases should concentrate in households that keep cattle, whatever their water source. Of the patients' households, 80% keep cattle within 100 m of the house, and ticks removed from those cattle carried the virus.

Scientist 3

No animal carries the virus. Infected cattle shed the virus in urine, which is washed into the river and into shallow household wells when fields are irrigated in summer. People are infected by drinking or bathing in that water. Households supplied with piped water from outside the valley should have few cases, however many cattle they keep. Virus genetic material was detected in 12 of 30 shallow wells sampled in August but in none of the same wells in March.

passage_title: Cracking Glass on a Building Facade
passage:
Three years after an office building opened, its tempered glass facade panels began cracking without being struck; within two years, 14 of 900 panels broke. All 14 were on the sun-facing south and west faces; an aluminum fin shades part of each panel for hours daily; 11 of the 14 failures occurred between 8 a.m. and noon; and all panels came from one production batch. Because tempered glass shatters completely, fracture origins were inferred from fragments left in the frame. Two students propose causes.

Student 1

The panels contain nickel sulfide inclusions, tiny stones formed in molten glass. Tempering freezes each stone in a high-temperature form; over several years it converts to a low-temperature form about 4% larger, and a stone in the panel's tensile core that expands this much cracks the glass. Warmth speeds the conversion, which is why the sunlit faces failed first. A stone that has nearly finished converting can be pushed over the threshold by any small added stress, including morning warming, so the hour of a break says little about its cause. Fragments from three failed panels showed a butterfly-shaped fracture origin near the panel's center around a dark particle, and 2 of 50 unbroken panels from the batch shattered when heated uniformly in an oven.

Student 2

The failures are thermal. Morning sun heats the exposed part of a panel while the fin-shaded strip and frame-covered edge stay cool; the hot center expands and pulls the cool edge into tension. Tempered glass resists this unless an edge was chipped during installation; the chip concentrates stress. Fracture origins should therefore lie at the edge nearest the fin's shadow, failures should peak in the morning, when the difference is greatest, and removing the fins should end the failures. Only sunlit faces experience such differences, which is why the north and east faces have no failures. Thermocouples on an intact south-facing panel recorded a 30 °C difference between its sunlit center and shaded edge at 10 a.m.

explanation: Student 2 reports that thermocouples "recorded a 30 °C difference between its sunlit center and shaded edge at 10 a.m." The numbers 4, 11, and 14 are the inclusion's percent expansion, the morning failures, and the total failures.
